key_terms.meaning: An engine where a spark plug ignites a premixed fuel-air mixture inside the cylinder.
An engine where fuel is injected into hot compressed air and ignites by itself.
Engine completing one cycle in four piston strokes and two crankshaft revolutions.
Air enters the cylinder at close to atmospheric pressure, with no blower or compressor.
Inside diameter of the cylinder, in metres or millimetres.
Distance the piston travels from TDC to BDC; L = 2 × crank radius.
r = (V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>) / V<sub>c</sub>, total cylinder volume divided by clearance volume.
Piston position farthest from the crankshaft, at minimum cylinder volume.
Piston position nearest the crankshaft, at maximum cylinder volume.
Flushing out burnt gases with fresh charge, done by ports in a two-stroke engine.
Spontaneous burning of the charge from high temperature and pressure, without a spark.
Opening a valve a few degrees of crank angle before TDC or BDC.
Crank-angle period when both inlet and exhaust valves stay open together.
The fixed sequence in which cylinders deliver power strokes, e.g. 1-3-4-2.
Ideal cycle using air as working fluid with heat added from outside instead of combustion.
Ideal cycle corrected for a real fuel-air mixture and specific heats that change with temperature.

takeaways: An IC engine converts chemical energy of fuel into work by burning the fuel inside the cylinder, and its types follow from separate choices such as ignition, strokes, cooling and aspiration.
Bore, stroke, TDC, BDC and compression ratio form the fixed vocabulary for every later calculation on power, efficiency and size.
A four-stroke engine gives one power stroke in two revolutions; a two-stroke engine gives one per revolution but needs port-based scavenging.
SI engines need a spark and a premixed charge; CI engines inject fuel into hot air and depend on autoignition and a high compression ratio.
Valve and port timing diagrams fix the real opening and closing of gas passages, so lead, lag and overlap explain why an engine breathes better than the simple cycle suggests.
Firing order and valve layout decide how smoothly power pulses reach the crankshaft and how the valves are driven.
Otto, Diesel and dual air-standard cycles allow a fair comparison of efficiency at fixed conditions because combustion is replaced by heat addition.

Fuel-air cycles and actual cycle analysis explain the gap between ideal efficiency and what the engine really delivers, through mixture strength, variable specific heats, gas exchange, heat loss and friction.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are usually marked for correct labelled sketches, precise definitions with symbols and the ability to compare ideal, fuel-air and actual behaviour rather than for a single final formula.

glossary.def: A heat engine in which fuel burns inside a closed cylinder and the expanding gases push a piston to produce work.
The travel of the piston between top dead centre and bottom dead centre.
The inner diameter of the engine cylinder.
The volume displaced by the piston in one stroke, equal to (π/4)d²L for one cylinder.
The small volume left above the piston when it is at top dead centre.
The ratio of total cylinder volume to clearance volume, written r.
A fictitious constant pressure that, acting over one stroke, would give the same work as the real cycle.
Power developed inside the cylinder, found from the indicator diagram.
Useful power measured at the crankshaft, after friction losses.
The process of pushing out burnt gases and filling the cylinder with fresh charge.
An opening in the cylinder wall uncovered by the moving piston to admit or release gas.
The crank-angle interval during which both inlet and exhaust valves are open.
The angle by which a valve opens before the piston reaches TDC or BDC.
The angle by which a valve closes after the piston passes TDC or BDC.
The order in which the cylinders of a multi-cylinder engine fire.
An ideal cycle in which air is the working fluid and combustion is replaced by heat addition from an external source.
An ideal cycle that accounts for a real fuel-air mixture and specific heats that vary with temperature.
Spontaneous ignition of the charge caused by high temperature and pressure rather than by a spark.
In the Diesel cycle, the ratio of volume after heat addition to volume before it, written ρ.
The ratio of actual air drawn in per cycle to the theoretical volume swept by the piston.
An engine that takes in air at atmospheric pressure without a compressor.
A compressor driven by the engine that raises intake air density above atmospheric.
The small gap in the valve train that allows for thermal expansion of valve parts.
Breakdown of burnt gases at high temperature into simpler species, which absorbs heat and lowers peak temperature.
